passage: At the school sports club, the coach split everyone into relay teams. Sarika, new this term, stood at the edge fiddling with her hearing aid. Nobody called her name. Mridul noticed she watched people's lips when they talked. He walked over and faced her directly. "Want to be on our team? You can run third." She nodded, surprised. Before the race, he tapped her shoulder instead of shouting when it was her turn to get ready. She ran fast. After, she said quietly, "Thanks for looking at me when you talk." Mridul grinned. "You're quick. Stay with us next week too."

qa.q: What did Sarika fiddle with at the edge?
qa.a: She was fiddling with her hearing aid.

qa.q: What might Sarika's quiet thanks suggest about how she had been feeling?
qa.a: It suggests she had felt left out and was relieved someone made it easier for her to join.

qa.q: Which of Mridul's choices helped Sarika join in?
qa.a: He invited her, faced her when speaking and tapped her shoulder instead of shouting.

qa.q: How might the team see Sarika after the race?
qa.a: They may see her as a fast teammate, not just the new girl.

grounding: It shows a child making room for a new, shy classmate with a hearing aid.

passage: I'm Sahil, and Vidya sits in front of me. When the new boy came to our class on crutches, most of us just stared. At lunch he sat alone near the steps, because our usual spot is on the grass slope. Vidya picked up her tiffin, walked over and sat next to him. The next day she asked our group to move to the steps. A few of us grumbled. She didn't argue; she just went. I don't know if she felt sorry for him or just liked him. By the end of the week, all of us were eating on the steps, and he was telling jokes.

qa.q: Where did the new boy sit alone at lunch?
qa.a: He sat alone near the steps.

qa.q: What does Sahil think might have been on Vidya's mind?
qa.a: Sahil isn't sure if she felt sorry for the boy or simply liked him.

qa.q: What small step made the biggest difference for the new boy?
qa.a: Vidya moving to eat beside him, and then asking the group to move to the steps.

qa.q: How is the new boy affected by the end of the week?
qa.a: He is no longer alone and feels comfortable enough to tell jokes.

grounding: A classmate observes a child making room for a new classmate with different abilities.

passage:
Day one: Lakshmi joined Class 6 from Kerala. She hardly spoke and ate lunch alone, staring at her book. Dilnaz saw her but didn't know what to say.
Day four: At recess, Dilnaz walked over with a skipping rope. "We need one more to hold the rope. Want to?" Lakshmi hesitated, then took the end.
Week three: Lakshmi taught the group a clapping game from her old school. Everyone got the rhythm wrong and laughed. Lakshmi laughed loudest. Dilnaz noticed she'd started saying "we" instead of "you all."

qa.q: What did Dilnaz bring when walking over on day four?
qa.a: Dilnaz brought a skipping rope.

qa.q: What does Lakshmi saying "we" instead of "you all" suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she now feels included and at home in the group, no longer an outsider.

qa.q: What could Dilnaz have done on day one?
qa.a: Dilnaz could have simply said hello or asked Lakshmi to join them at lunch.

qa.q: How does Lakshmi's clapping game change the group?
qa.a: The group enjoys something new she brings, which makes her a contributor, not just a newcomer. 😊

grounding: It shows a child including a shy new classmate over several weeks.

passage: Come, kanna, sit. When I was ten, a new girl joined our school in Madurai. Her name was Sarika, and she walked with two wooden crutches. At break, all of us ran to play kho-kho and she sat alone on the step, turning her bangles. Nobody was mean. We just forgot her. After three days I felt so bad I couldn't eat my lemon rice. So I went and asked, 'I'm Lavanya. Will you be our timekeeper? You have a watch.' She shouted the times louder than our teacher! Later we made up a sitting game with pebbles so she could win too. Sarika and I wrote letters to each other for forty years. That is what making room means, kanna.

qa.q: What job did young Lavanya offer Sarika at break?
qa.a: Lavanya asked Sarika to be the timekeeper for kho-kho because Sarika had a watch.

qa.q: Why couldn't young Lavanya eat the lemon rice?
qa.a: Lavanya felt guilty that everyone had forgotten Sarika, who sat alone on the step for three days.

qa.q: Which of young Lavanya's ideas worked, and why?
qa.a: They gave her a real role in the game and then invented a pebble game where she could play and win too.

qa.q: How might Sarika have felt on those first three days at break?
qa.a: She probably felt lonely and left out, sitting by herself while everyone ran off to play.

grounding: An elder recalls making room for a new classmate who used crutches.

passage: Rain hammered the tin roof, so PE moved into the crowded school hall. Forty children shouted at once. Vikas noticed Deepak, the new boy with the hearing aids, standing by the wall looking lost. Sir had explained the relay rules, but in this noise Deepak had clearly caught nothing. Vikas walked over and stood right in front of him so Deepak could see his face. 'Relay. Run, touch the wall, come back, tap the next hand,' he said slowly, and showed it with his arms. Deepak nodded and grinned. 'Our team?' 'Our team,' said Vikas. When Deepak got tapped, he ran like wind. Afterwards he said, 'Thanks. Nobody faces me.'

qa.q: Where was PE held that day, and why?
qa.a: It was held in the crowded school hall because rain was hammering the roof.

qa.q: What does Deepak's comment 'Nobody faces me' suggest about how he felt before?
qa.a: It suggests he often felt lonely and left out, because people spoke without letting him see their faces, so he missed things.

qa.q: What small step made the difference for Deepak?
qa.a: Vikas stood face to face, spoke slowly and showed the rules with gestures before inviting him onto his team.

qa.q: What would have changed if Vikas hadn't walked over?
qa.a: Deepak would likely have stayed by the wall, confused about the rules and left out of the relay.

grounding: Shows a child including a new classmate with a hearing difference despite a noisy setting.

passage:
On Pradeep's first day at the school in Andheri, he sat alone at the back. He wore a small hearing aid behind one ear, and when the class laughed at a joke, he looked around, lost.
Imran, ten, noticed. At lunch he sat opposite Pradeep, not beside him, so Pradeep could see his face. He spoke clearly, not shouting.
“Cricket after lunch. You want to bat?”
Pradeep hesitated. “I can't always hear the calls.”
“Then we'll use hands. Thumbs up for run, flat palm for stay.”
That afternoon Pradeep hit a four. Imran gave him the loudest thumbs up on the ground.

qa.q: Where did Imran sit at lunch?
qa.a: He sat opposite Pradeep, not beside him.

qa.q: How did Pradeep feel when the class laughed and he looked around?
qa.a: He felt lost and left out, not able to catch the joke.

qa.q: What did Imran do that made Pradeep feel included?
qa.a: He sat where Pradeep could see his face, spoke clearly and invented hand signals for the game.

qa.q: How might the other boys see Pradeep after the four?
qa.a: They probably see him as a good teammate, not as the new boy who sits alone.

grounding: A ten-year-old makes room for a new classmate who uses a hearing aid.

passage:
“Quiz teams! Groups of four,” said Ms Nair.
Everyone ran to their friends. Aditi, who had moved from Guwahati a month ago, stayed at her desk, looking at her pencil.
Yogesh, eleven, looked at his group. “We need one more.”
“Take Farhan,” said Rohit.
“Farhan's already with them.” Yogesh walked to Aditi's desk. “Want to be on our team?”
Aditi looked up. “I'm not very good at quizzes.”
“You know about Assam, right? There's always a geography round.”
She smiled a little. “I know about rhinos.”
“Perfect. Come on.”
In the geography round, Aditi answered two questions nobody else knew.

qa.q: How long ago had Aditi moved from Guwahati?
qa.a: A month ago.

qa.q: How was Aditi feeling when everyone ran to their friends?
qa.a: She felt shy and left out, staying at her desk looking at her pencil.

qa.q: What made Yogesh's invitation work?
qa.a: He asked her directly and pointed to something she knew, so she felt she had something to offer.

qa.q: How does Rohit see the team choice differently from Yogesh?
qa.a: Rohit only thinks of friends already picked, while Yogesh notices the new girl sitting alone and makes room for her.

grounding: An eleven-year-old invites a shy new classmate into a quiz team.

passage:
On our class trip to the Lodhi Garden, the plan was a treasure hunt across the lawns and up the steps of the old tomb. I was excited until I saw Tushar looking at the steps from his wheelchair.
I'm Chaitanya. I went to Ms Kapoor and asked if we could change the game. “What if the clues are only on the paths? And teams take turns reading the map?”
She said yes. Tushar read the map for our team. He was fast.
We didn't win. But at the end Tushar said it was the first trip where he didn't just watch. I felt proud of that, more than a prize.

qa.q: Where was the class trip?
qa.a: To the Lodhi Garden.

qa.q: How did Chaitanya feel at the end of the trip?
qa.a: Chaitanya felt proud that Tushar joined in rather than watched, more than about any prize.

qa.q: What did Chaitanya do that helped include Tushar?
qa.a: Chaitanya asked the teacher to change the game so the clues were on the paths and teams took turns reading the map.

qa.q: How did the change affect Tushar?
qa.a: He felt included and useful, saying it was the first trip where he didn't just watch.

grounding: A student adapts a group game so a classmate who uses a wheelchair can take part.

passage:
Class 4 teacher's note, second week of term.
Shankar joined us on Monday. He uses crutches after a leg surgery and is still getting used to the stairs. On the first two days he ate lunch alone near the classroom door while the others ran to the ground.
On Wednesday, Nikita noticed. She asked me if she could bring a board game to the corridor at lunch. She invited Shankar and three others. They played ludo, and Shankar won twice.
Today Nikita asked if the class could play word games on the ground's steps, so Shankar can join from the bottom step.
I've said yes, and will add it to the timetable.
— Mrs Kulkarni

qa.q: What game did Nikita's group play in the corridor?
qa.a: Ludo.

qa.q: What might Nikita have been feeling when she noticed Shankar eating alone?
qa.a: Nikita probably felt concerned and sorry for Shankar, sitting alone while everyone ran off.

qa.q: What did Nikita do that made room for Shankar?
qa.a: She chose games he could join, brought them to where he could get to, and invited others too.

qa.q: How might Shankar feel when Nikita invites him?
qa.a: Shankar likely feels relieved and welcome, not left out by his crutches.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a child making lunch-break games accessible to a new classmate on crutches.

passage:
Dear Diary,
There's a new girl in our class, Trisha. She came from Shillong. She doesn't talk. At lunch she sits at the end of the bench and reads a book with her tiffin still closed.
Today I saw the book. It was about volcanoes. I love volcanoes!
I sat next to her and said, "Is that the one with the Iceland volcano?" She looked up, surprised, and nodded. Then she showed me a picture. Then she opened her tiffin.
Tomorrow I'm going to ask her to sit with our group. Rahil might say she's weird. I'll say she knows more about volcanoes than him.
— Yogesh

qa.q: Where did Trisha come from?
qa.a: Shillong.

qa.q: What was Trisha feeling when she looked up, surprised?
qa.a: Trisha felt surprised and a little shy, but pleased that someone shared her interest.

qa.q: What small step helped Yogesh reach Trisha?
qa.a: Starting with the book she was reading gave them something in common to talk about.

qa.q: If you were Trisha, what would you want from the class?
qa.a: Trisha would probably want patience and someone to sit with, without being pushed to talk a lot.

grounding: A child writes about welcoming a shy new classmate through a shared interest.

passage:
The kho-kho game at the village school was about to start. Disha, who walks with a limp, sat on the wall as always.
Arohi ran over. "Come play."
"I'm too slow. They'll catch me in a second."
Arohi thought. "Then be the one who sits in the line. You don't have to run far. You just have to watch and jump up when tapped."
Disha hesitated, then took a spot in the sitting line. When Arohi tapped her, she sprang up and caught a boy who thought she wouldn't move.
The whole team cheered. Disha grinned so wide her eyes closed.

qa.q: Where did Disha usually sit during kho-kho?
qa.a: On the wall.

qa.q: What was Disha feeling when she said she was too slow?
qa.a: Disha felt unsure and worried she would be caught quickly and let the team down.

qa.q: What did Arohi do that made room for Disha?
qa.a: She found a role in the game that suited Disha instead of just asking her to run like everyone else.

qa.q: How might the boy who was caught see Disha now?
qa.a: The boy is surprised and may now see Disha as a real player, not someone who just watches.

grounding: A village child finds a way to include a classmate with a limp in kho-kho.

passage:
On Noa's first Monday at the school in Rotterdam, she stood by the fence at break, holding her lunchbox with both hands. She had moved from Haifa and knew about ten words of Dutch. Ines watched her for a while from the four-square court. Then she walked over, bounced the ball twice and held it out.
"Play?" she said, and pointed at the chalk squares.
Noa shook her head, then looked at the ball again. Ines showed the rules with her hands instead of talking: one bounce, hit it into another square, out if it lands on a line. The first time Noa missed, nobody laughed, because Ines missed the next one on purpose. By the bell, Noa was shouting "Line!" in Dutch.

qa.q: Where did Noa stand at break on her first Monday?
qa.a: Noa stood by the fence at break, holding her lunchbox with both hands.

qa.q: What was Noa probably feeling at the fence, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Noa was probably shy and nervous about joining in, because she held her lunchbox tightly and shook her head at first.

qa.q: Which of Ines's choices made it easier for Noa to join?
qa.a: Showing the rules with her hands instead of words, and missing a shot on purpose so Noa's mistake did not stand out, made joining feel safe.

qa.q: What is it like for Ines when Noa finally shouts "Line!" in Dutch?
qa.a: Ines probably feels glad and a bit proud, because her small effort turned a lonely new girl into a player in one break time.

grounding: Shows a child making room for a shy new classmate who does not yet share the language.

passage:
The week before Diwali, Class 5 was making paper lanterns for the school corridor. The room was loud: scissors, glue, everyone talking at once. Yash sat at the end of the table cutting strips alone. He wears hearing aids, and when three people talk together he watches faces hard and still misses most of it.
Ganga noticed he had cut his strips too short because he had not heard the change in size. She did not say it across the table. She moved her chair next to his, turned so he could see her face, and held up the teacher's sample.
"Longer, like this," she said slowly, not loudly.
Yash grinned and started again. After that, Ganga tapped his shoulder before she spoke, and the whole table started doing it too. 🪔

qa.q: What was Class 5 making the week before Diwali?
qa.a: Class 5 was making paper lanterns for the school corridor.

qa.q: Why might Yash have been sitting alone and cutting quietly?
qa.a: Yash may have felt left out and a little frustrated, because in the noisy room he watched faces hard and still missed most of the talk.

qa.q: How could a teacher build on what Ganga started?
qa.a: The teacher could ask groups to face each other and take turns speaking, so Yash can follow without having to ask every time.

qa.q: What changes for the rest of the table once everyone starts tapping Yash's shoulder?
qa.a: The others learn a simple habit that makes the group work better, and Yash becomes part of the talk instead of someone they talk around.

grounding: Illustrates a child adjusting how the group works so a classmate with hearing aids can take part.

passage:
This is Swati, from the back row of the winter carol choir.
The new girl joined in December. She stood half behind the curtain and mouthed the words without singing. Most of us didn't notice. Devika did.
On the second day Devika asked Sister to let the altos stand in a curve instead of a straight line, "so everyone can hear each other". I think it was really so the new girl wasn't stuck at the end. Then Devika gave her the spare song sheet with the tricky lines underlined in pencil.
I can't say what the new girl felt. She didn't talk much. But by the Christmas concert she was singing loud enough that I could hear her from my place, and she walked out of the hall next to Devika, laughing.

qa.q: How did Devika ask the altos to stand?
qa.a: Devika asked Sister to let the altos stand in a curve instead of a straight line.

qa.q: Why does Swati think Devika wanted the altos in a curve?
qa.a: Swati suspects Devika was concerned the shy new girl felt stuck and left out at the end, though Swati can only guess from what she saw.

qa.q: What small step helped the new girl most, and why?
qa.a: The underlined song sheet helped, because it let her learn the tricky lines privately instead of being corrected in front of everyone.

qa.q: How might the new girl remember Devika's help at the concert?
qa.a: She may remember feeling welcomed rather than watched, since Devika made room without making a fuss about her being new.

grounding: Shows a classmate, seen from outside by an observer, quietly making room for a shy newcomer.

passage:
Monday, first week of winter term: the new boy, Tushar, walked in on crutches. At break the class played kho-kho, and he sat alone on the steps. Chandrika saw him but ran to her team.
Wednesday: it was cold and foggy, and kho-kho moved indoors. Chandrika noticed Tushar watching every move. She sat beside him. "You know the rules better than us." He shrugged. "I watch a lot."
The next Monday, Chandrika asked Ma'am if Tushar could be the referee and chaser-caller. He blew the whistle and shouted calls sharper than anyone. At the end, two boys argued about a tag, and they both turned to him. "Tushar, was it out?"
He grinned. "Out." Chandrika laughed. Nobody argued.

qa.q: What game did the class play at break?
qa.a: The class played kho-kho.

qa.q: What was Tushar likely feeling sitting alone on the steps?
qa.a: Tushar was likely lonely and left out, watching a game he knew well but wasn't part of.

qa.q: What small step made the biggest difference for Tushar?
qa.a: Chandrika sitting with him, noticing what he was good at, and asking the teacher for a role that fit him.

qa.q: How do the other boys come to see Tushar?
qa.a: They come to trust his judgement, turning to him to settle an argument, so he becomes part of the game.

grounding: Shows a child making room for a new classmate who uses crutches by finding a real role for him.
